pass_a_gloss: Book 2, Tomes 5. Tome 1. [Lemma, Isaiah 10:33-34:] Behold indeed the Master, Lord Sabaoth, will confound the glorious with strength, and the lofty in insolence will be crushed, and will be humbled, and the lofty will fall by sword, and Lebanon with the lofty will fall. In the finished book the discourse was about the things of the Assyrians and of the one administering the realms of the Persians, marching against Judaea and Jerusalem, and suffering unexpectedly the things from divine wrath. For Israel was saved beyond expectation, not stretching a bow, not snatching a shield, not [leading] a horseman, not with art leading out against his phalanxes, not by law of war overpowering the hand of the opponents, but in power of God and grace. For an angel of the Lord went out, it says, and killed in one night from the camp of the Assyrians a hundred eighty-five thousands. And this having happened clearly, those expecting to perish were dancing, and were bringing up to the God who saved them the thank-offering songs, saying this: At evening weeping will lodge, and toward the morning gladness. And besides these: You turned my lament into joy for me, you tore my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness. But the bold and haughty one, and crying that great and vanishing [boast], I will seize the whole inhabited world with the hand like a nest, and like eggs left behind I will lift it, and there is none who will escape me or speak against me, was convicted of having thought great of himself in vain. For he ran away scarcely, and a fugitive moved home, leaving Judaea. Therefore also the God of all was saying: Do not fear, my people, those dwelling in Zion, from Assyrians. And the manner of the flight too was being described, all but shaking cities and villages by his passing. And again: Fear will take Ramah, city of Saul. And interpreting such things, we have made the narration more historical, but not outside the truth. For in some way it is every necessity that the discourse of the interpretation be fitted suitably to the quality and force of the things set before us. But since it is a custom of the God-inspired Scripture, through things done quickly and historically, to make plain sometimes the mysteries, and to mould images of hidden thoughts, we say that the inventor of sin tyrannized against us, and upon the [peoples] of the S[aviour] [the section breaks off mid-word].
pass_b_english: Book II, in five tomes. Tome 1.

“Behold, the Master, the Lord of Hosts, will throw the glorious into confusion with strength; the lofty will be crushed in their insolence and brought low; the lofty will fall by the sword, and Lebanon will fall with its lofty ones” (Isaiah 10:33–34).

In the book just completed, our discussion concerned the Assyrians and the one who ruled the realms of the Persians, who marched against Judea and Jerusalem but unexpectedly suffered what came from divine wrath. For Israel was saved beyond all expectation: not by stretching a bow, not by snatching up a shield, not by leading out horsemen or skillfully setting forces against his phalanxes, not by overpowering the enemy’s hand by the law of war, but by the power and grace of God. For “the angel of the Lord went out,” it says, “and killed in one night one hundred and eighty-five thousand from the camp of the Assyrians” (Isaiah 37:36).

When this had plainly happened, those who had expected to perish danced for joy and offered songs of thanksgiving to the God who had saved them, saying: “Weeping will lodge for the evening, and gladness comes in the morning” (Psalm 30:5). And besides this: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Psalm 30:11).

But the bold and arrogant one, who shouted that great and empty boast, “I will seize the whole world in my hand like a nest, and like eggs left behind I will take it up, and there is no one who will escape me or speak against me” (compare Isaiah 10:14), was shown to have thought great things of himself in vain. For he barely escaped, and leaving Judea he withdrew home a fugitive. That is why the God of all said: “Do not be afraid of the Assyrians, my people who dwell in Zion” (Isaiah 10:24). The manner of his flight was also described, as he all but shook cities and villages as he passed. And again: “Fear will seize Ramah, the city of Saul” (compare Isaiah 10:29).

In interpreting such passages, we made our account rather historical, yet not outside the truth. For it is in every way necessary to fit the language of interpretation to the character and force of what lies before us. choices.why: Book I of the commentary ended with the Assyrian invasion and its overthrow.

choices.english: not by leading out horsemen or skillfully setting forces against his phalanxes
choices.why: The string of negatives stresses that Israel was saved by God, not by skill in war.
ἐξίτηλος is what fades away; Sennacherib's boast came to nothing.
Cyril admits the account so far kept to the history before turning to the spiritual sense.
Cyril's name for the devil; kept as written.
